Paper: Kingma and Welling (2013), [Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114).
The central contribution is a practical stochastic gradient estimator for variational learning with continuous latent variables, together with an amortised inference network.
The [VAE study note](../../study-notes/machine-learning/autoencoders.qmd#vae) develops the encoder, decoder, CVAE, Gaussian KL, and implementation details.

## Problem

A latent-variable model generates an observation $x$ by first drawing an unobserved code $z$ and then drawing $x$ conditional on that code.
Its joint and marginal densities are

$$
  p_\theta(x,z)=p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z),
$$

$$
  p_\theta(x)=\int p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)\,dz.
$$

The prior $p(z)$ is a chosen component of the model, often a standard Gaussian.
The decoder network parameterises $p_\theta(x\mid z)$, and the integral sums the contributions of all possible latent explanations.
With a nonlinear decoder, both this marginal likelihood and the model posterior $p_\theta(z\mid x)$ are generally intractable. [Paper, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3).

The posterior is exact relative to the specified model; calling it the true posterior does not imply that the model equals the real data-generating process.
Likewise, a continuous density value is not the probability of observing one exact point.
Latent variables can provide a compact representation, but lower dimension is not a defining mathematical requirement of a VAE.

## Previous attempts

An ordinary autoencoder learns a deterministic code and a reconstruction map, but its reconstruction objective alone does not provide a prior for generating new examples.
Variational inference instead introduces a tractable distribution $q_\phi(z\mid x)$ to approximate the posterior and optimise a likelihood lower bound.
The difficulty is efficiently differentiating the expectation when the sampling distribution itself depends on learned parameters.
The paper addresses this difficulty with a reparameterised estimator and a recognition network that shares inference parameters across examples. [Paper, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=2).

## Proposed solution

The encoder outputs a distribution over latent vectors, while the decoder outputs a distribution over observations.
For a fixed observation, define the evidence lower bound $B$ by

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  B(x)&=\mathbb E_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}
  [\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]\\
  &\quad-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\Vert p(z)).
  \end{aligned}
$$

Training maximises this bound, or equivalently minimises reconstruction negative log-likelihood plus latent KL.
The KL to the prior belongs inside the objective; the KL to the model posterior measures the remaining variational gap. [Paper, Eqs. (1)–(3)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: distinguish the two KL terms"}

Write $q_x=q_\phi(z\mid x)$ and use Bayes' rule inside the posterior KL:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_x\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x))
  &=\mathbb E_{q_x}\left[
  \log\frac{q_x(z)}{p_\theta(x,z)}\right]\\
  &\quad+\log p_\theta(x).
  \end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging gives the exact gap identity

$$
  \log p_\theta(x)-B(x)
  =D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_x\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x)).
$$

Factoring the joint density inside $B$ produces the reconstruction expectation and the KL to the prior.
Nonnegativity of the posterior KL gives the lower bound, assuming the distributions have the required support and finite expectations.

:::

For a diagonal Gaussian encoder, the reparameterisation is

$$
  z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon,
  \qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
$$

Noise is sampled from a fixed distribution, and the resulting latent vector is a differentiable function of the encoder outputs.
Monte Carlo averages of the reconstruction term and, when available, an analytic KL yield the stochastic gradient variational Bayes estimator. [Paper, §§2.3–2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3).

At generation time, sample $z$ from the prior and use the decoder; an encoder requiring an observed $x$ is unnecessary for unconditional generation.
This differs from reconstruction, where the encoder conditions on a supplied example.

## Evidence

The paper evaluates latent-variable models on MNIST and Frey Face data and compares variational bounds and learning behaviour with alternative inference methods.
Its experiments support the practicality of stochastic gradient variational learning in the tested models, while latent-space visualisations illustrate learned generative structure. [Paper, §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=5).

## Limitations

A diagonal Gaussian posterior can be too restrictive, and the ELBO remains separated from the log-likelihood when the approximate posterior is inaccurate.
The reconstruction likelihood is a modelling choice: Bernoulli, Gaussian, and Laplace decoders imply different reconstruction losses.
A KL penalty does not guarantee interpretable coordinates or that every prior sample decodes well.
The next inference question is therefore how to obtain a richer posterior without losing tractable sampling and density evaluation, which motivates [normalizing flows](normalizing-flows.qmd).

## Connections

[ACT](../action/act.qmd) uses a CVAE for demonstrated action chunks, with a weighted KL term and a specific choice of zero latent code at deployment.
[DDPM](ddpm.qmd) also admits a variational bound, but its latent variables form a scheduled corruption chain rather than one learned encoder code.
[GANs](gan.qmd) learn a sampling map through an adversarial objective, illustrating that generative learning does not always mean directly maximising a tractable likelihood.
